name: Data Act
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: large Commission forecasts, critical legal-economic analyses, one industry readiness survey; no ex-post evidence (applied from September 2025)
summary: The Data Act gives users of connected devices and businesses rights to access and share data, and has applied since September 2025. The Commission forecast EUR 270 billion of extra GDP by 2028, but nothing has yet been measured, and economists at Bruegel, CERRE and universities argue the access rules are weak or complex. A 2025 survey found almost no German firms ready, and the Commission has already proposed amendments in its November 2025 Digital Omnibus.

indicators.objective: The proposal has no LFS indicator section; the memorandum relies on the Data Market Monitoring study, an SME panel consultation five years after adoption, data-spaces monitoring and an evaluation (now due by 12 September 2028). The Act has applied only since 12 September 2025

indicators.indicator: EU-27 GDP +1.98 percentage points by 2028 (press release: EUR 270bn additional GDP by 2028); +2.2m jobs; government revenue +EUR 96.8bn and investment +EUR 30.4bn (2024-2028)
indicators.evidence: Not measured; obligations applied only from September 2025 (design obligations from 2026). No ex-post estimate exists. Critics (Kerber, Martens) argue the access mechanism is weak, making the forecast doubtful.

indicators.objective: Data access for users and third parties
indicators.indicator: Value of B2B/B2C data access from connected products up to EUR 196.7bn a year by 2028; contractual fairness +EUR 7.4bn a year (SME profits +EUR 5.2bn)
indicators.evidence: Not measured. A German industry survey 100 days before application found only 1% of companies had fully and 4% partly implemented the Act; 52% thought it did not apply to them.

indicators.indicator: Fair access to cloud and edge services: +EUR 7.1bn a year
Manufacturers' access infrastructure EUR 410m one-off + EUR 88m a year; contractual fairness EUR 69m a year; B2G EUR 552.5m one-off + EUR 78.1m a year
indicators.evidence: Not measured. The November 2025 Digital Omnibus proposes amendments (e.g. on trade-secret refusals and business-to-government data requests in public emergencies) and claims savings of at least EUR 1bn a year across the digital acquis.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact assessment report accompanying the Data Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2022) 35), SWD(2022) 34
literature.title: Impact assessment report accompanying the Data Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2022) 35)
literature.outcomes: GDP; jobs; data-access value; compliance costs
literature.headline: Preferred option raises EU-27 GDP by 1.98 percentage points by 2028 and creates 2.2m jobs; benefits up to EUR 196.7bn a year from IoT data access, EUR 7.4bn from contractual fairness, EUR 7.1bn from cloud switching; one-off costs EUR 410m for manufacturers and EUR 552.5m for B2G
literature.summary_plain: The Commission forecast that giving users and businesses rights to device data would add about 2% to EU GDP by 2028 at modest cost.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Data Act: Commission proposes measures for a fair and innovative data economy (press release), IP/22/1113, 23 February 2022
literature.title: Data Act: Commission proposes measures for a fair and innovative data economy (press release)
literature.headline: New rules expected to create EUR 270 billion of additional GDP by 2028
literature.summary_plain: The headline promise: EUR 270 billion of extra GDP by 2028.

literature.citation: Kerber (2023), Governance of IoT Data: Why the EU Data Act Will not Fulfill Its Objectives, GRUR International 72(2): 120-135
literature.title: Governance of IoT Data: Why the EU Data Act Will not Fulfill Its Objectives
literature.headline: Act correctly identifies manufacturers' de facto exclusive control of IoT data, but its user-access mechanism is likely weak and largely ineffective because it protects data holders' control too strongly; it will not achieve its goals of empowering users and unlocking data for innovation
literature.summary_plain: An economist argues the Data Act leaves device makers in control of the data, so it is unlikely to deliver the promised innovation.

literature.citation: Martens (2023), Pro- and anti-competitive provisions in the proposed European Union Data Act, Bruegel Working Paper 01/2023
literature.title: Pro- and anti-competitive provisions in the proposed European Union Data Act
literature.headline: Access and portability rights weaken manufacturers' de facto monopoly over product data, but the Act gives them a de jure right to monopolistic pricing of data transfers, bans using data to build competing products and bars transfers to DMA gatekeepers; fuzzy definitions add uncertainty
literature.summary_plain: A Bruegel economist finds the Data Act both opens up device data and protects manufacturers in ways that could hold back competition.

literature.citation: Krämer (coord.), Colangelo, Richter & Schnurr (CERRE) (2023), Data Act: Towards a Balanced EU Data Regulation, CERRE report, March 2023
literature.title: Data Act: Towards a Balanced EU Data Regulation
literature.headline: Supports a new data-portability style access right but calls for simpler, clearer rules; recommends limiting B2G sharing to ad hoc access with cost-based compensation; warns of complexity and legal uncertainty
literature.summary_plain: A CERRE expert group backed the Data Act's aims but warned its rules were complex and uncertain, and proposed simplifications.
literature.interested_party: CERRE is funded partly by industry members, including large digital firms

literature.citation: Bitkom (2025), Data Act: Kaum Unternehmen vorbereitet (survey of 605 companies), Bitkom press release, 20 May 2025
literature.title: Data Act: Kaum Unternehmen vorbereitet (survey of 605 companies)
literature.method: survey (605 German firms with 20+ employees, March-April 2025)
literature.headline: Only 1% of companies had fully and 4% partly implemented the Data Act; 10% had just started, 30% had not started; 52% believed it did not apply to them
literature.summary_plain: Months before the Act applied, almost no German companies were ready and half thought it did not concern them.
literature.interested_party: Bitkom is the German digital industry association and lobbied on the Act

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Proposal for a Digital Omnibus Regulation (amending Regulation (EU) 2023/2854), COM(2025) 837
literature.title: Proposal for a Digital Omnibus Regulation (amending Regulation (EU) 2023/2854)
literature.headline: Folds the Data Governance Act, Free Flow Regulation and Open Data Directive into the Data Act and amends it; claims savings of at least EUR 1bn a year plus EUR 1bn one-off across the package; Data Act evaluation by 12 September 2028
literature.summary_plain: Barely two months after the Data Act applied, the Commission proposed amending it and merging other data laws into it to cut red tape.
